doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Goodman exhibit, Hymie Shertzer, radio shows and Teddy Wilson at the Cookery
summary: Meeting Hymie Shertzer, doing WBAI radio interviews, and going with Teddy Wilson to the Goodman Quartet reunion at the Waldorf.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: But that was a combination of a biography and a discography. And he had a book out called BG on the Record Benny Goodman on the Record. And I found it in a local library and I started writing him post cards about like where can I find the alternate take of “House Hop” or something like this. Because in those days it was hard to find, I mean there’s no internet, there’s no nothing in the record stores and all this kind of stuff, and so I was very much enmeshed in collecting and getting to meet the musicians who had worked with Goodman. Well when we were preparing for the Goodman exhibit, Hymie Shertzer came in and Hymie had been the lead alto player in Benny Goodman’s band back in the 30s. And he really couldn’t believe that like some kid knew who he was. And someone else came into the Jazz Museum, and I can’t remember his name but he was on WBAI radio, here in New York, a Pacifica station. And they did really kind of like esoteric programming and very leftish at that time. And somehow he said would you like — it was kind of weird to find this 14, 15-year-old kid that wants to hear this old music. I came on his radio show just to talk about the Jazz Museum and he offered me a little — a few shows of my own. So I interviewed Hymie Shertzer and then I interviewed Ray Nance when I was about 15 or so. And I said some of the stupidest things. I have a cassette of it somewhere, just horrible. You’ll never hear them. But the bottom line was so already this interest in history — so I met Benny Goodman at that exhibit thing when I was 15, and around the same time, when we were going to hear Teddy Wilson play with my parents, Teddy was playing at a place called the Cookery, which was at 9th Street and University Place, which was owned by Barney Josephson, who used to own Café Society. And then in the early 70s he had Alberta Hunter made her comeback at this club, and Teddy Wilson played there, and all kinds of people. Well my parents took me down to see Teddy Wilson one night, this is all happening in these years. And Teddy had a tuxedo on, and the date, I’m not one of those date people but I happen to remember it because I can picture it, it’s either 1972 or ’73. I think it was ’72. And Teddy is dressed in a tuxedo which he never wore. I said, “Oh Mr. Wilson, why are you wearing a tuxedo.” He said well they’re giving a — the National Urban League is giving an award to Lionel Hampton tonight at the Waldorf, and I’m going from here to there, and we’re re-uniting the original Benny Goodman Quartet will be playing. And I couldn’t believe it. You
